claims.text: Local residual stresses generated during composite solidification govern the unresolved stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-expansion mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr generates local residual stresses during solidification.
Residual stresses produce microstructural heterogeneity that modifies tensile creep, cold-rolling hardness, elastic modulus, and aging-induced hardening.
Homogenization followed by slow cooling will reduce the residual effects of differential thermal contraction.
Residual internal stress fields arising from differential thermal expansion produce local microsegregation.
Residual internal stress fields produce dislocation-pinning sites.
Thermal-expansion-induced stresses promote heterogeneous microstructural development and alter phase distribution.
The stress-induced heterogeneous microstructure alters dislocation mobility.
Reducing residual microstress by homogenization and slow cooling will lower tensile creep rates at 1250 °C relative to the as-cast alloy.
Homogenization and slow cooling will diminish the increase in microhardness caused by cold rolling relative to the as-cast alloy.
Homogenization and slow cooling will produce more uniform elastic moduli from 293 K to 1100 K relative to the as-cast alloy.
Homogenization and slow cooling will reduce hardening after aging at 600–800 °C relative to the as-cast alloy.
The standard as-cast alloy contains significant residual stresses caused by uncontrolled thermal-expansion mismatch.
The proposed mechanism applies only while thermal expansion during solidification is the dominant factor controlling behavior.

A lack of statistically significant differences in creep rate, modulus uniformity, cold-work hardening, and aging hardening between treated and as-cast samples would falsify the proposed governing-cause hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mediator and mechanism invoke residual-stress-generated dislocation pinning, which implies inhibited dislocation motion, but the prediction states that reducing those stresses and pinning sites will lower the 1250 °C creep rate. The direction of the creep prediction is not reconciled with the proposed pinning mechanism.
